sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Three agent-written books stalled at my own review
sections.para: In August agents on graphs.sgit.ai wrote three books, about 100,000 words, for a long flight. They were good and much of their method now runs this newsroom, but they stayed at v0.3.0, v0.2.0 and v0.1.0 because the seven-stage review's approve stage was me, and nothing ever passed it.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Small finished pieces beat one big review stage
sections.para: Written on 26 August for a flight, the three books total 47 chapters and three print PDFs with anchored claims. An altitude ladder, a board and the book as a graph surrounded them, and the making-of read far better. They stalled at review, while roles, versions and per-article graphs live on here.

sections.label: How they started
sections.line: A flight deadline shaped three books in one day
sections.para: graphs.sgit.ai was built from 21 August to 20 September 2026 around the idea that a node means nothing without its edges. On 26 August a memo asked for three books to read on a flight, so each became one self-contained 60 to 120 page PDF, written by three parallel Claude Code sessions.

sections.label: The three books
sections.line: An argument, a making-of and an atlas, all unfinished
sections.para: Meaning Through Connectivity, v0.3.0, argues the idea in 15 chapters, 38,824 words and 119 pages. Creating a Book Using Agentic Workflows, v0.2.0, has twelve chapters, 31,435 words and 92 pages from 88 releases. The held Universe volume, v0.1.0, is an atlas of 90 concepts, 168 verbs and 165 quotes.

sections.label: The experiments around them
sections.line: The experiments around the books matter more than them
sections.para: An altitude ladder compressed a book to five levels, down to 135 words, and exposed two contradicting sentences forty pages apart. A book was decomposed to the word and rebuilt byte-identical, so edits become graph transformations. Worked example vaults and a team of seven roles with verbatim founder memos completed the set.

sections.label: Why one book read better
sections.line: The book written over a real record read better
sections.para: The making-of was aligned "by orders of magnitude" better than the graphs book. Same agent, same day: one was written over 41 release rows, 38 verbatim briefs and a searchable repository, the other over an argument. Articles here are now that kind of record, which is why books can be made from them.

sections.label: Where it stopped
sections.line: Review as change control stalled waiting on me
sections.para: A board of eight workstreams, 40 tasks and seven stages per change was built, and both change-control workstreams blocked on the same person. Nothing passed the approved stage, and the last release was 20 September. Like my unfinished Leanpub books, the workflow suited quality but not momentum, with the biggest step waiting on me.

sections.label: What lives on here
sections.line: Much of the books' method now runs this newsroom
sections.para: This newsroom borrowed the seven roles, the "where we lose" disclosure, readable versions per article, a graph per document, llms.txt with markdown twins, and memos kept verbatim as source material. The state map went the other way, from this newsroom to graphs.sgit.ai, as ideas move between sites once proven.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: The books are unfinished and the comparison is single
sections.para: Two books are under review, one is held and one is frozen. The flight notes are not published, only recorded as a bunch of notes. The workflow was right for quality but needed smaller steps, and the comparison is one case: two books, one agent, one day.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: a voice memo and graphs.sgit.ai's published record
sections.para: The article came from my voice memo of 16 October 2026. Everything else is from graphs.sgit.ai as published that day: the books, the altitude ladder, the book as a graph, the board, the team, the release history and founder memos 38, 39, 40, 42 and 44, with page counts measured from the PDFs.
